description:
I’m a final-year BSIT student from Pakistan, interested in Python, AI/ML, data science, and web development. I’m working on Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data, a project using satellite and environmental data to support smarter crop rotation and agricultural decisions.

Looking for teammates skilled in Python, GIS/remote sensing, NASA Earthdata, data analysis, machine learning, or agriculture. Seeking motivated, collaborative people ready to contribute and build an impactful solution!
summary:
RotateWise: A NASA-Powered Crop Rotation Advisor

What we developed: RotateWise is a free, mobile-friendly decision-support web app that helps farmers anywhere compare crop rotations. A farmer chooses a region (or enters their own climate data), their current rotation, water access, soil, equipment, market access and priorities. The app compares four strategies, including the existing one, and explains each with benefits, risks, evidence and data gaps.

How it addresses the challenge: It uses NASA POWER climate data to show rainfall, heat, frost risk, dry months and bare-field periods. It includes scenario sliders, a field risk map, a 5-year soil health outlook and a confidence score that tests each rotation across 20 simulated climate futures. It explains scientific terms and reminds users that local experts must validate results.

Why it matters: Droughts, heat and declining soils threaten food security worldwide, and good local advice is often slow or unavailable. RotateWise gives any farmer a fast, transparent first comparison that protects soil and water and supports, not replaces, farmer judgment.
details:
What it does and how it works
RotateWise is a free, mobile-friendly web app that helps farmers compare crop rotations. The farmer chooses a region (8 built-in regions on 4 continents, or their own climate data), their current rotation, water access, soil texture, equipment, market access and priorities such as saving water, income, nitrogen fixing or erosion control. The app uses NASA POWER climate data (temperature and rainfall) to work out growing windows, dry months, frost-risk months, hot months and bare-field periods. It then compares four rotation strategies, including the existing one. Each is scored out of 100 and explained with why it was suggested, its benefits, the risks to check locally, the evidence behind it and the data gaps. A robustness test re-scores every rotation in 20 simulated climate futures and shows how often it stays the top choice.

Main features
Climate signal page and monthly water balance; field calendar showing bare soil, with cover crops filling the gaps; vulnerable-season warnings; 5-year soil health outlook; field risk map (erosion, water stress, frost pockets); rainfall and warming scenario sliders; a Learn page explaining NDVI, evapotranspiration, soil moisture anomalies and frost risk; a downloadable PDF action plan; settings saved on the device with no login; dark mode; keyboard and screen-reader friendly design.

Benefits and intended impact
Farmers get a fast, transparent first comparison of options before committing land and money. It lowers the barrier to practices that protect soil and water, and it gives them clear questions to ask local agricultural experts. Because it works with custom climate data, it can be used anywhere in the world.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework); inline SVG for charts and the field map; NASA POWER API (T2M temperature and PRECTOTCORR rainfall) fetched with a Python script; jsPDF for the PDF plan; GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. I used an AI assistant (Claude) to help plan, write and test the code, and I reviewed and checked the results myself.

What makes it creative
Cover crops fill the bare months automatically, and a confidence score shows uncertainty instead of one overconfident answer. A side-by-side field map compares the existing rotation with the top match, and the tool is built around the farmer’s own priorities and constraints.

Factors I considered
Accessibility and low-bandwidth use on phones; being honest about limits (crop ratings are simplified, climate is one representative point per region, and the field map is a schematic); and making it a support tool that never replaces local expertise. Planned next steps include SMAP soil moisture, MODIS NDVI, GRACE-FO groundwater and optional farm accounts.
